title: Episode 3: Rachel Thomas on AI Product Management
speaker: Rachel Thomas
content:
Lenny: Rachel, you co-founded fast.ai and now lead AI product at a major tech company. How is AI product management different?

Rachel: The fundamental difference is uncertainty. Traditional PM: you define requirements, engineers build, you ship. AI PM: you define the problem, but the 'how' involves probability, not certainty. You're managing a stochastic system.

Lenny: What does that change in practice?

Rachel: Three things. First, evaluation becomes product work. You need eval sets, human feedback loops, automated metrics. Second, you ship 'good enough' and improve via feedback - the product gets better with usage. Third, failure modes are different - hallucination, bias, edge cases that don't exist in deterministic software.

Lenny: How do you prioritize AI features?

Rachel: I use a modified framework: User Value × Technical Feasibility × Data Readiness / Risk. Data Readiness is new - do we have the data to train/evaluate? Risk includes regulatory, reputational, safety. Most AI projects fail at Data Readiness or Risk.

Lenny: What about RAG vs fine-tuning?

Rachel: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) should be your default. It's cheaper, more controllable, citeable, and updates instantly. Fine-tune only when: 1) You need specific style/tone that prompting can't achieve, 2) You have 10k+ high-quality examples, 3) Latency/cost requirements demand it. 90% of use cases don't need fine-tuning.

Lenny: How do you handle hallucination in user-facing products?

Rachel: Defense in depth. 1) RAG with citations - every claim traceable. 2) Confidence thresholds - don't show low-confidence outputs. 3) Human-in-the-loop for high-stakes. 4) User feedback buttons (thumbs up/down) to catch errors. 5) Monitoring dashboards for hallucination rates.

Lenny: What's your advice for PMs transitioning to AI?

Rachel: Learn the basics: embeddings, vector search, prompt engineering, evaluation. You don't need to train models, but you must understand capabilities and limits. Take fast.ai's Practical Deep Learning course. And partner deeply with ML engineers - they're your co-PMs on AI products.

Lenny: What's the future of AI products?

Rachel: Compound AI systems - multiple models, tools, and retrievers working together. Not one big model, but orchestrated workflows. Also, AI-native interfaces - chat is just the beginning. We'll see generative UI, proactive agents, and ambient intelligence. The PMs who understand this will build the next generation of products.
